chapters.title: Chapter 3: Duration: Measuring Interest Rate Risk

lessons.title: Macaulay Duration: The Weighted-Average Time to Get Your Money Back

children.text: In the last lesson you saw three separate rules: longer maturity, lower coupon and lower yield all make a bond more sensitive to rate changes. Juggling three rules is clumsy. Is a 12-year 9% bond riskier than an 8-year zero? You cannot say from the rules alone. In 1938, economist Frederick Macaulay solved this with a single number that folds all three rules together. SEBI's duration-based debt fund categories, from ultra short duration to long duration, are all defined using it. This lesson shows you how to calculate it by hand and what it really measures.

body.text: Macaulay duration is the average time, in years, until you receive a bond's cash flows, where each payment is weighted by its share of the bond's present value. It is the centre of gravity of the bond's value in time.

children.text: The Idea: A Weighted Average of Time

markDefs.definition: The present-value-weighted average time to receive a bond's cash flows, measured in years. Named after Frederick Macaulay, who introduced it in 1938.

children.text: A 5-year bond does not make you wait five years for your money. Coupons arrive every six months, so some money comes back in half a year, some in a year, and the big payment at the end.

asks: on average, how long do you wait? It weights each payment date by how much of today's price that payment represents. A tiny coupon in year 1 barely pulls the average; the large final payment pulls it hard.

body.caption: PV(CF_t) = present value of the cash flow in period t, P = price (sum of all PVs), t ÷ m = time of that cash flow in years, m = coupons per year.

children.text: Picture a see-saw laid along a timeline. Each cash flow is a weight sitting at its payment date, and the size of each weight is its present value. Macaulay duration is the point where you would place the pivot to balance the see-saw.
Worked Example: The 7.10% Bond from Chapter 1

Return to the illustrative 7.10% G-Sec with exactly five years left, priced at a 6.80% yield. You already calculated each present value and a price of ₹101.25. Now add two columns: each cash flow's weight (its PV divided by the price) and weight multiplied by time.

body.caption: Macaulay duration of a 7.10% G-Sec, 5 years left, at a 6.80% yield (per ₹100 face value)

body.title: Share of the Bond's Value Arriving at Each Date (%)

children.text: The nine coupons together carry just under 27% of the bond's value and pull the average forward by 0.70 years. The final payment carries 73% and dominates. So although you wait five years for the last rupee, the value-weighted average wait is 4.30 years.

body.title: Calculate a Macaulay duration
body.prompt: An illustrative 3-year NCD pays an 8% annual coupon and trades at par (₹100) at an 8% yield. Its cash flows are ₹8, ₹8 and ₹108 at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. What is its Macaulay duration in years? Round to two decimal places.

children.text: How Duration Captures All Three Risk Drivers
Recalculate duration for the bonds from the previous lesson, and every one of the three rules shows up in a single number.

body.caption: Macaulay duration of illustrative 10-year bonds (semi-annual coupons)

children.text: Lower coupon, longer duration. Lower yield, longer duration. And the ranking matches the price sensitivities you calculated in Lesson 1 exactly: the zero-coupon bond fell most and has the longest duration; the 9% bond fell least and has the shortest. Duration is the unifying measure of interest rate risk.

body.text: A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration always equals its maturity, because it has only one cash flow and that payment carries 100% of the weight. A 10-year STRIPS has a duration of exactly 10 years. Every coupon-paying bond has a duration shorter than its maturity.

children.text: Duration and Maturity Are Not the Same Thing

For coupon bonds, duration rises with maturity but never keeps pace. Stretch a 7% coupon bond priced at a 7% yield from 10 to 100 years and its duration only doubles. It approaches a hard ceiling, the duration of a bond that pays coupons forever.

body.title: Macaulay Duration vs Maturity at a 7% Yield (years)

body.label: Maximum possible duration for any 7% coupon bond priced at a 7% yield
body.context: The duration of a perpetual bond: (1 + 0.07 ÷ 2) ÷ 0.07. A 50-year bond reaches 14.31 years and a 100-year bond 14.77.

body.title: Where the perpetual bond ceiling comes from

children.text: A bond that pays coupons forever and never repays principal has a Macaulay duration that depends only on its yield, not on its coupon. As maturity grows, a coupon bond looks more and more like this perpetual bond, because the principal repayment moves so far out that its present value shrinks towards zero. That is why the 7% coupon line in the chart flattens out. It also explains a warning from Chapter 2: bank AT1 perpetual bonds have no maturity, so their duration and rate risk are very high whenever the market stops assuming they will be called.

content.caption: In years, with y = annual yield and m = coupons per year. At 7% semi-annual: 1.035 ÷ 0.07 = 14.79 years. At 9%: 1.045 ÷ 0.09 = 11.61 years.

body.title: Duration beats maturity
body.question: All four illustrative bonds are priced at a 7% yield and pay semi-annual coupons where applicable. Which has the longest Macaulay duration?
body.explanation: The 6-year zero has a duration of exactly 6.00 years. The 8-year 12% bond, despite the longest maturity, has a duration of only about 5.71 years because its large coupons return value early. The 7-year 7% bond is about 5.65 years and the 5-year 9% bond about 4.17 years. Maturity alone would have picked the wrong bond.

children.text: Where You Meet Macaulay Duration in India

SEBI's 2017 categorisation of mutual fund schemes defines most debt fund categories by the Macaulay duration of their portfolio. A short duration fund must keep it between 1 and 3 years, a medium duration fund between 3 and 4 years, and a long duration fund above 7 years. Every debt fund factsheet discloses the portfolio's Macaulay duration alongside its YTM. Lesson 5 of this chapter shows you how to read those numbers together.

In Excel or Google Sheets, =DURATION(settlement, maturity, coupon, yield, frequency, basis) returns Macaulay duration in years for any settlement date. For our bond: =DURATION(DATE(2026,9,15), DATE(2031,9,15), 7.10%, 6.80%, 2, 4) returns 4.30.

body.title: Name the special case
body.textWithBlank: A bond whose Macaulay duration exactly equals its maturity must be a ___ bond.
body.explanation: With only one cash flow at maturity, all of the value-weight sits at the maturity date, so the weighted-average time equals the maturity.

body.title: Meera's seven-year goal
body.scenario: Meera Joshi, a 42-year-old HR head in Pune, needs a known sum in about seven years for her son's postgraduate studies. Her adviser shortlists three illustrative options: (A) a 10-year G-Sec with a 7.50% coupon at a 7.20% yield; (B) an 8-year SDL with a 7.20% coupon at a 7.30% yield; (C) a 7-year zero-coupon G-Sec STRIPS. Meera assumes option B is closest to her goal after C, because its maturity of 8 years is nearest to 7.
body.prompt: Using Macaulay duration, which option's interest rate exposure best lines up with Meera's seven-year horizon? Explain why maturity alone misled her, and what she should keep in mind.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Macaulay durations: (A) 10-year 7.50% G-Sec ≈ 7.24 years; (B) 8-year 7.20% SDL ≈ 6.21 years; (C) 7-year STRIPS = 7.00 years exactly.
2. The STRIPS matches her horizon precisely: one cash flow, on the date she needs it, with no coupons to reinvest and no need to sell early.
3. Surprisingly, the 10-year G-Sec (7.24 years) sits closer to her horizon than the 8-year SDL (6.21 years). Maturity misled her because the SDL's coupons pull its average cash flow timing well inside eight years, while the 10-year bond's longer life pushes its duration out to about seven.
4. Why duration matters for a goal: as Chapter 2 showed, falling rates hurt reinvestment but raise bond prices, and rising rates do the reverse. When a bond's duration matches the holding period, those two effects roughly offset, so the value at the goal date is more predictable. Chapter 5 develops this into immunisation.
5. Cautions: (a) Duration changes as time passes and yields move, so a coupon bond match needs periodic checking. (b) Option A must be sold at year 7, at whatever price the market offers then, and the offset between price and reinvestment effects is only approximate. (c) She should confirm that STRIPS in the size she needs are actually available to her through her platform, and compare the yields on all three before deciding.

cards.definition: The present-value-weighted average time to receive a bond's cash flows, in years.
Its present value divided by the bond's price.
Always less than maturity. Longer for lower coupons and lower yields.
(1 + y ÷ m) ÷ y. The ceiling a coupon bond approaches as maturity lengthens.
=DURATION(settlement, maturity, coupon, yield, frequency, basis) returns Macaulay duration in years.

points: Macaulay duration is the value-weighted average time to receive a bond's cash flows: the centre of gravity of its value in time.
Calculate it by weighting each payment date by that payment's present value as a share of price, then adding up.
The 7.10% five-year bond at 6.80% has a Macaulay duration of 4.30 years, because 73% of its value arrives at maturity.
Duration captures all three risk drivers: lower coupons, lower yields and longer maturities all lengthen it.
A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity; a coupon bond's is always shorter and has a ceiling as maturity grows.
SEBI defines its duration-based debt fund categories by Macaulay duration, and Excel's DURATION function calculates it directly.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Bonds, yields and investors are illustrative. Duration is a model-based measure that changes as time passes and yields move. SEBI category definitions can be revised, so check the current scheme information document. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
